To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ZFPIP, a new type of homeodomain cofactor, is able to bind to PBX1 protein and to inhibit the binding of HOX/PBX complexes to DNA.
we have identified and characterized a new PBX-interacting protein, ZFPIP, that contains zinc finger domains and prevents the interaction of PBX1 with its cofactors.

we have identified a new type of partner of the transcription factor PBX1, that contains zinc finger domains, and that inhibits the binding to DNA of HOXA9, another homeodomain transcription factor that interacts with PBX1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of a new type ZFPIP protein that interacts with PBX1.
the identification of new proteins that are able to interact with PBX1.
the identification of novel PBX1 partners, their functional characterization and their role during development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ZFPIP could be involved in PBX1 functions in several tissues during development and that it could act as a general modulator of PBX activity by interfering with the binding of HOX/PBX complexes to DNA.
PBX1 is a key player in the control of gene transcription during development, in particular in the control of HOX gene activity.
the ZFPIP protein is a novel type of partner for PBX1 that may be involved in the regulation of PBX1 function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ZFPIP acts as a negative regulator of PBX1 activity.
ZFPIP could act as a repressor for PBX1 function.
ZFPIP could participate in the modulation of PBX1 transcriptional activity by preventing HOXA9-PB1 binding to DNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the identification of new PBX1 partners will be useful to better understand the molecular mechanisms of PBX1 action.
PBX1 can bind to several types of transcription factors, including non-homeodomain ones, and that this diversity of interaction could be important to modulate its function during development.
ZFPIP can act as a negative regulator of PBX1 function and that this mechanism may be important during female genital tract and other developmental pathways.
